name: Rib flare correction / diaphragm breathing

card.summary: Breathing and core drills aimed at pulling protruding lower ribs back in; popular in posture circles, with almost no direct trial evidence on appearance.
card.aka: Rib flare fix, rib cage tucking, 360 breathing, zone of apposition training
card.note: A visibly prominent rib cage can also reflect structural conditions (scoliosis, pectus), which breathing drills are not described as treating.

quick.overview:
Rib flare describes lower ribs that stick out forward or sideways, most visible in side view or when the arms are raised. Fitness and physical-therapy writers commonly link it to posture, core weakness and chest-dominant breathing, and looksmaxxing forums discuss it as something that can spoil the torso silhouette.

The correction approach centres on diaphragmatic breathing and core-bracing drills meant to lower the rib cage over the pelvis. Descriptions come largely from physical-therapy and fitness sources; no controlled trial found tests breathing drills for changing visible rib prominence in otherwise healthy people.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is that the diaphragm and deep abdominal muscles control how the lower ribs sit. Proponents say retraining exhalation and core engagement restores the contact zone between diaphragm and ribs and lets the ribs rest lower. A related clinical-commentary literature describes asymmetrical rib and pelvic positioning treated with specific respiratory exercises.
quick.risks: The exercises themselves are low-impact and generally regarded as low risk. The main caveat reported in the sources is that flared or prominent ribs can accompany scoliosis, pectus excavatum or other structural conditions, which are assessed by clinicians and managed differently, including surgically in some pectus cases.

lead: Rib flare correction is the practice of using diaphragmatic breathing, core engagement and posture work to bring protruding lower ribs down and back so the torso looks narrower and tighter at the waist-to-chest transition. People who do it want a cleaner front profile, a flatter lower rib line in photos and a more V-shaped upper body. Rib flare is a descriptive term, used mainly in physical therapy, fitness and posture communities, for lower ribs that angle outward or forward rather than sitting flush with the abdomen. It is generally described as a postural pattern rather than a disease, although similar-looking rib cage prominence can accompany structural conditions such as scoliosis or pectus excavatum.[1][2]

Practitioners describe the approach as retraining the diaphragm and abdominal wall so the lower ribs sit lower during breathing and standing. The anatomy behind it is textbook: the diaphragm's costal part arises from the inner surface of the lower ribs, the lower ribs swing outward in a 'bucket handle' motion during inhalation, and in forceful exhalation the abdominal muscles pull the lower ribs down.[8][14][15] Proponents argue that when breathing is shallow and chest-dominant and the abdominals are not engaged, the lower ribs ride up and out.[1] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed alongside pectus excavatum as a torso-aesthetics concern, with attention to shirtless appearance, bodybuilding waist width and photo profile.[1][3]

No clinical trial found has tested breathing exercises specifically for reducing visible rib flare in healthy people. Related literature consists of radiographic measurement of rib cage deformity in scoliosis, a clinical commentary on respiratory exercises for asymmetrical trunk posture, surgical series on pectus repair, and a broader literature on diaphragmatic breathing for lung disease, sleep and relaxation.[4][5][6][7][10][11] Physical-therapy descriptions summarised by Grokipedia say that non-pathological cases often improve within weeks of consistent core and breathing work, while acknowledging that rib-flare-specific randomised trials are limited.[1]

paras: Descriptions of rib flare, mostly from physical-therapy and fitness writing, characterise it as the lower ribs (roughly ribs 7 to 10) angling outward and upward, creating a visible edge at the front or side of the torso, sometimes on one side only and often described as more common on the left.[1] Grokipedia's summary lists suggested contributing factors including weak core muscles, prolonged sitting, chest-dominant breathing, stress-related breathing patterns, anterior pelvic tilt, an exaggerated lumbar curve, adolescent growth spurts, heavy overhead pressing or bench arching, genetics and postpartum changes, and notes that it is not generally painful on its own.[1]

The infrasternal angle, the angle at which the costal margins meet at the front, is sometimes used to describe a wide or narrow lower rib cage; the same source suggests that an angle well above about 90 degrees can indicate flare.[1] It adds that the look is more visible in lean people, when lying down or reaching overhead, and during or after pregnancy, and that in bodybuilding it can make the waist look wider.[1] Anatomical references note that ribs 8 to 10 are 'false' ribs attached indirectly to the sternum through the cartilage above, a flexibility that supports the bucket-handle movement of breathing, and that rib count and attachment vary between individuals.[14]

Wikipedia describes the diaphragm as a dome-shaped muscle whose costal part arises from the inner surface of the lower ribs (7 to 10) via their cartilages, with further attachments at the xiphoid process and lumbar vertebrae. When it contracts it moves downward and enlarges the thoracic cavity; when the central tendon is fixed, it can instead lift the ribs, widening the chest laterally and upward.[8] Forced exhalation uses the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles as antagonists to the diaphragm.[8] Wikipedia's breathing article adds that in forceful breathing the abdominal muscles pull the lower ribs down and push the diaphragm up, and that deep breaths build intra-abdominal pressure that supports the spine, which is why lifters are often taught to breathe in before heavy lifts.[15]

According to the physical-therapy explanation summarised in Grokipedia, the abdominal wall muscles (transversus abdominis and obliques) attach to the costal margin. When breathing relies on the upper chest and accessory muscles, or when the abdominals are not engaged, the lower ribs are said to ride up and out, shrinking the zone of apposition, the region where the diaphragm lies against the inner rib cage.[1] Related structures named in the same account include pelvic tilt and thoracic curvature, with a 'left anterior interior chain' pattern describing an asymmetry among trunk, ribs, pelvis and hips.[1]

A clinical commentary in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy describes that pattern of asymmetry and presents a side-lying respiratory exercise combined with a hip adductor pull-back as a way to address it.[7] It is a clinical application paper rather than a controlled trial. The zone of apposition has itself become a measurement site in diaphragm ultrasound research, where its excursion and thickening fraction can be recorded, but those studies concern respiratory function rather than rib appearance.[16]

In general terms, practitioners describe diaphragmatic or three-dimensional breathing that expands the lower ribs sideways and back while keeping the front of the rib cage down, paired with abdominal engagement during exhalation and exercises such as planks and dead bugs. Hands-on techniques and postural awareness are also mentioned in physical-therapy descriptions.[1] Individual programmes vary widely and are not standardised.

Grokipedia's account groups the approaches into core work, glute and hip-flexor work to address pelvic tilt, posture awareness during sitting, breaks from prolonged sitting, physical-therapy techniques such as the side-lying respiratory exercise, chiropractic rib and soft-tissue work, and biofeedback or rehabilitative ultrasound to observe abdominal muscle thickness; it also mentions Pilates and yoga for prevention.[1] Self-checks described there include a mirror check of whether the ribs sit forward of the hip line, feeling the infrasternal angle, and lying on the back with knees bent to see whether the lower ribs lift on a full exhale; it states these are for awareness only, not diagnosis.[1]

The Cleveland Clinic's general description of diaphragmatic (belly) breathing involves slow inhalation through the nose so the abdomen rises while the chest stays still, followed by exhalation through pursed lips with the abdominal muscles tightening; it suggests practising lying down first, then sitting.[9] The clinic lists relaxation, lower heart rate and blood pressure, reduced work of breathing and better muscle function during exercise as claimed benefits and notes it is not meant to be the only treatment for people with conditions such as COPD, asthma or anxiety.[9] It does not discuss rib flare or appearance.

Lifters use a related idea: forum posts on T Nation describe breathing into the diaphragm and using the pressure of a deep belly breath to brace the trunk against a belt.[17] Breath-focused training also appears in yoga, tai chi and other traditions listed in the breathing article.[15]
No studies found testing breathing or core exercises as a means of reducing visible rib flare in otherwise healthy people.

Related research includes a 2026 retrospective study in Spine Deformity of 40 adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients and 20 controls that proposed a radiographic measurement called rib flare distance to quantify axial rib cage deformity; it showed excellent inter- and intra-observer reliability (ICC 0.986 and 0.993) and discriminated patients from controls (AUC 0.941). This concerns measurement of a structural deformity, not an exercise outcome.[5][16] A 2024 paper in Heliyon examined markerless 3D pose estimation from a single camera for quantifying exercise movement, a technology study rather than a test of rib flare correction.[4] A 2026 retrospective series of 72 pectus patients described surgical bridging-bar techniques for aesthetic and functional results.[6]

Studies of breathing exercises in other populations exist but address different outcomes, such as a network meta-analysis of breathing exercises in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [10], and a three-arm randomized trial in 99 older adults comparing diaphragmatic breathing relaxation training with cognitive-behavioral therapy for sleep quality [11].

For the abdominal wall, a 2014 systematic review summarised on Wikipedia found that exercising during and after pregnancy may reduce the gap in diastasis recti, that core strength training may help postpartum, and that corrective exercises focus on drawing the abdominal muscles in rather than pushing them out.[13]

Rib cage prominence can accompany scoliosis, where it is associated with pulmonary function and cosmetic appearance according to the rib flare distance study, and pectus excavatum, a sunken breastbone.[5][12] Clinicians treat these through assessment and, where indicated, bracing or surgery. Exercise-based rib flare programmes are described in the sources as aimed at postural rib position, not at these structural conditions.

Pectus excavatum affects an estimated 1 in 150 to 1 in 1,000 births, is about three times more common in males, and is evaluated by visual exam and imaging, with the Haller index used to grade severity. Treatment ranges from observation to posture and chest-strengthening exercise, the vacuum bell (introduced in 2006), and surgery such as the Ravitch technique (1949) and the Nuss procedure (first performed in 1987); the article also notes embarrassment, social anxiety and reduced self-esteem among people with the condition, and silicone implants or fat grafting for appearance.[12]

Diastasis recti, a widened gap between the rectus abdominis muscles, is common after pregnancy and often narrows within about eight weeks; Grokipedia lists it, along with hyperlordosis, scoliosis and costochondritis, among conditions that can look like or accompany rib flare, and says postpartum rib expansion linked to relaxin typically recovers over months.[1][13] Persistent or severe chest or back pain, or breathing difficulty, is described there as a reason to seek medical advice.[1]

A long guide on looksmax.org covers fixing pectus excavatum and rib flare, with sections on what the conditions are, proposed solutions and cited studies. Its author describes having pectus himself and writes for others dealing with it.[3] Discussion in these communities treats the rib cage as part of torso proportion and shirtless appearance, and rib flare is often raised alongside waist width, vacuum-pose and posture topics.[3]

Outside looksmaxxing, the same vocabulary circulates in physical-therapy clinics, yoga and Pilates instruction, postpartum recovery and powerlifting, where attention to rib position under the bar and bracing is a common coaching theme.[1][17]

timeline.event: The Ravitch technique for surgical repair of pectus excavatum is introduced.[12]
The Nuss minimally invasive pectus procedure is first performed.[12]
The vacuum bell for non-surgical pectus treatment is introduced.[12]
A clinical commentary describes the right side-lying respiratory left adductor pull-back exercise for trunk asymmetry.[7]
A systematic review reports exercise may reduce the gap in diastasis recti.[13]
A comprehensive guide to fixing pectus excavatum and rib flare circulates on looksmax.org.[3]
A network meta-analysis ranks breathing exercises for COPD; a single-camera 3D pose estimation paper is published.[4][10]
A randomized trial compares diaphragmatic breathing training with CBT for sleep quality in older adults.[11]
The rib flare distance radiographic metric for scoliosis is proposed and a 72-case pectus bridging-bar series is published.[5][6][16]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, rib flare is usually discussed together with pectus excavatum as a correctable torso flaw, with guides proposing exercise-based fixes.[3]

claims.claim: Rib flare can be corrected with exercises and breathing retraining
claims.believers: Guide authors on looksmax.org present non-surgical solutions for pectus and rib flare and say they can answer questions on fixing them.[3]
claims.experts: Physical-therapy descriptions summarised in Grokipedia say core strengthening and diaphragmatic breathing retraining often improve rib position, but no controlled trial of this for visible appearance was found.[1]

claims.claim: Rib flare comes from weak core and poor breathing mechanics
claims.believers: Posture-focused users attribute protruding lower ribs to chest-dominant breathing and an inactive abdominal wall.[1]
claims.experts: A clinical commentary describes asymmetrical trunk and rib patterns linked to respiratory and pelvic mechanics, while radiographic research shows rib cage deformity in scoliosis is a distinct structural problem.[7][5]

claims.claim: Exercise can also fix pectus excavatum
claims.believers: The forum guide treats pectus excavatum and rib flare as fixable together.[3]
claims.experts: Surgical literature describes operative repair, for example bridging-bar pectus procedures, for suitable patients; no trial found shows exercise reversing the sunken sternum.[6]

claims.claim: Rib flare is fixed in weeks by breathing and core work
claims.believers: Physical-therapy descriptions and forum posters say non-pathological cases improve with consistent exercise, with severe cases taking months.[1][3]
claims.experts: The same summary acknowledges that rib-flare-specific randomised trials are limited and that much of its support is clinical guidance and case-level reports.[1]

claims.claim: Lifting and posing habits cause rib flare
claims.believers: Lifters and bodybuilders attribute a wide-looking waist to heavy overhead pressing, excessive bench arch and a flared rib position.[1]
claims.experts: Physical-therapy sources list imbalanced training among contributing factors; no trial was found measuring rib position against lifting technique.[1]

claims.claim: Diaphragmatic breathing improves bracing and torso control
claims.believers: T Nation lifters describe belly-breath bracing against a belt as a way to stabilise the trunk.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that deep breaths build intra-abdominal pressure that supports the lower spine, which is why lifters are told to breathe in before heavy lifts.[15]

claims.claim: Rib flare and pectus excavatum are the same problem with the same fix
claims.believers: The looksmax.org guide treats them together.[3]
claims.experts: Pectus excavatum is described as a congenital sternal depression whose treatments range from observation and exercise to vacuum bells and surgery; Grokipedia calls it different from functional rib flare.[1][12]

angle.text: Physical therapy descriptions say that rib position is influenced by how the diaphragm and abdominal wall share the work of breathing, so retraining them is proposed to bring the ribs down and give a tighter-looking midsection.[1] Forum guides use the same logic for appearance.[3]
